stories.title: DayOne said to weigh options including delay, size cut for US IPO after data-centre rout
stories.summary: It has not made a final decision and may still move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks

stories.content:
It has not made a final decision and may still move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks

\[HONG KONG\] DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US initial public offering, including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases, according to people familiar with the matter.

While Singapore-based DayOne has been waiting for the right window to launch the IPO, it has also been considering the possibility of pushing back the share sale until the market recovers, the people said.

Other options include going ahead with a smaller listing that may raise US$2.5 billion to US$3 billion, roughly half of what it had originally aimed for, the people said.

DayOne, whose backers include Coatue and Hillhouse, is continuing to engage with potential investors and still wants to move forward as soon as the market allows, the people said.

The company was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter, people familiar with the matter said previously. It had been eyeing a valuation of about US$20 billion, the people have said.

Deliberations are ongoing and DayOne has not made any final decisions, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

The company could still opt to move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks, according to the people. DayOne declined to comment.

While data centres have drawn global investor demand amid a boom in sectors related to artificial intelligence, a more negative sentiment has started to have ripple effects on IPOs.

DayOne has been raising billions of dollars in private funding rounds as it seeks capital to build out its pipeline.

Australian data centre company Firmus Grid pulled its roughly US$5 billion IPO when investors balked at the valuation it sought, while AirTrunk, which also operates data centres, delayed a planned real estate investment trust IPO in Singapore to 2027.

South Korean digital infrastructure company Elice plunged 32 per cent in its Seoul trading debut on Tuesday (Oct 20).

Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, and Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News has reported.

On Wednesday, shares of Australian data centre operator Nextdc plummeted after it cut earnings guidance.

Some investors are hoping that the recent market volatility will pass after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. They are also looking ahead to the performance of Anthropic’s upcoming listing as an important gauge of sentiment towards the AI sector.

DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier in October. The offering is being led by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup.

IFR reported on Monday that DayOne was gathering more investor feedback before launching the share sale.

DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain. Other backers include GDS Holdings, the SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Microsoft scraps UK data centre deal with Nscale, Telegraph says
stories.summary: The facility’s site has been contending with a series of delays, the newspaper adds

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
The facility’s site has been contending with a series of delays, the newspaper adds

\[LONDON\] Microsoft has pulled out of a UK data centre deal with British neocloud Nscale at a critical time for the startup’s initial public offering hopes, the *Telegraph* reported.

The newspaper did not provide a specific reason for why the US tech giant had pulled the plug on the deal in Loughton, Essex, though it said the site has been contending with a series of delays.

Authorities have told Nscale they do not expect a power supply to the facility until the 2030s, it added.

Nscale’s flagship site in Norway is also six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts (MW) of the intended 30 MW data centre up and running.

Nscale relies on Microsoft and Anthropic for around 85 per cent of its contracts, going by an IPO filing, and the former had been set to become the anchor tenant at Nscale’s first British data centre in Essex.

Microsoft’s withdrawal would mark a setback for the company that is seeking to raise as much as US$3 billion in an IPO as soon as October, and which was already contending with investor jitters over the risks of the wider artificial intelligence build-out.

Nscale is one of the most prominent neoclouds, a new group of companies seeking to build huge computer complexes for AI.

They want to cash in on the hundreds of billions of dollars big tech companies have pledged to spend on the technology and are a key part of the AI boom’s supply chain.

An Nscale spokesperson told the *Telegraph*: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

Microsoft did not comment to the *Telegraph* and did not immediately respond to queries by Bloomberg.

The backdrop to Nscale’s IPO ambitions has turned gloomier in recent days, with fellow neocloud CoreWeave in the spotlight last week after the co-founder said the company was exploring ways to borrow in investment-grade debt markets, where there are vast pools of money from insurers to tap.

Investors had already grown cautious of AI computing suppliers due to the tens of billions of dollars they and their customers are borrowing to finance the massive build-out of data-centre capacity.

CoreWeave shares plunged in the first three sessions of the week, then bounced back somewhat, before concern returned on Friday, leading to the the stock’s worst week since November with a 25 per cent drop.

That also came in the wake of Australian data centre company Firmus scrapping its plans for an IPO, after the deal failed to garner enough support for the marketed share price. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Anthropic IPO filing warns of AI data center risks
stories.summary: Anthropic's IPO filing highlights potential scrutiny for AI data centers due to environmental and social concerns. The company anticipates regulatory hurdles and public controversy regarding power and water use.
stories.content:
Anthropic PBC expects to face increased scrutiny regarding environmental and social tensions from AI infrastructure development, according to its initial public offering (IPO) filing on Monday.The company noted that efforts to secure power may encounter regulatory hurdles. This is due to perceptions that its activities affect utility costs or the environment.Data center development has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny, focusing on environmental impact, land, and water use. Anthropic's brand is also subject to scrutiny over perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety impacts.Oracle Corp. cited force majeure last month after environmental opposition and regulatory setbacks complicated power procurement. This was for a data center campus in New Mexico intended for OpenAI.Anthropic's S-1 filing also identified climate change and broader environmental concerns as risk factors. Higher average temperatures can increase power consumption and water usage for cooling equipment, raising operating costs.Blaine Townsend, director of sustainable, responsible and impact investing at Bailard, stated that AI's risks and opportunities are now core financial and fiduciary considerations. Bailard's research highlights AI's environmental footprint in three categories: data centers in burdened communities, AI's water use, and energy demand.Some states have considered moratoriums on new data center builds. This is to assess the potential impact on the environment and power prices. Anthropic acknowledged that such backlash could result in reputational harm.The company also noted increasing scrutiny related to its ESG practices and reporting, both in the United States and internationally. This focus includes AI's power intensity, public concern about water usage, and reliance on critical minerals. Investors may use these factors to guide investment strategies, potentially choosing not to invest if ESG policies are deemed inadequate.

stories.title: Data center boom tests smaller US communities
stories.summary: Data center expansion offers investment to smaller US communities. However, it also tests their capacity to support power-intensive developments and secure lasting economic benefits.
stories.content:
Data center expansion is creating investment opportunities in smaller US communities, according to a report by the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility and Heartland Forward. This growth also tests their ability to support power-intensive developments and secure lasting economic benefits, the report said.Factors such as utility capacity, workforce availability, water resources, and infrastructure cost allocation determine whether a project strengthens the local economy. These elements can also determine if residents are left with expenses that outlast the initial building boom.
### Evaluating Investment Impact

"Attracting investment and generating lasting economic value are not necessarily the same thing," Dominic Williams, a senior expert at McKinsey and report author, told Data Center Knowledge. He advised local leaders to consider all costs and benefits, not just headline capital expenditure or job announcements.Sean Farney, vice president of data center strategy at JLL, noted that the search for sites is expanding data center investment geographically. Power constraints, community opposition, and market saturation in larger cities are pushing developers towards alternative locations like Abilene, Texas, and Fort Wayne, Indiana.Farney highlighted the economic benefits beyond construction, including spending on ongoing operations, hotels, restaurants, and housing. He also mentioned tax revenue and infrastructure improvements as components communities should evaluate.Ruthbea Yesner, group vice president for worldwide public sector at IDC, stressed the importance of scrutinising which benefits remain local. She stated that power, broadband, and water are the deciding factors, rather than land or tax incentives.Yesner cautioned against communities overextending themselves by accepting projects before utility commitments for upgrades are secured. She also advised assessing water availability and workforce capacity before development proceeds.
### Securing Long-Term Benefits

Yesner recommended using written infrastructure commitments and public reporting on resource consumption. Safeguards against stalled projects include incentive clawbacks and cost-overrun sharing arrangements.Williams similarly suggested linking incentives to verified investment milestones and defining developer responsibilities for infrastructure upgrades. He added that infrastructure investments should serve broader local needs, not just a single development.Workforce partnerships between developers, community colleges, and local employers can create pathways into technical occupations. Procurement arrangements can also create opportunities for local suppliers.These measures help connect individual projects with broader development priorities. "The ultimate measure of success is not simply whether a community attracts a major project, but whether that investment leaves the local economy more competitive, resilient, and better positioned for future growth," Williams said.

stories.title: UK Government misses data center planning policy deadline
stories.summary: The UK Government has missed its deadline for consulting on new national planning policy for data centres. Ministers have not yet specified when the proposals, intended to clarify planning decisions, will be published.
stories.content:
The UK Government has missed its self-imposed deadline for consulting on a new national planning policy for data centres.Ministers have not yet stated when the long-awaited proposals will appear, according to a parliamentary answer.In November 2025, the government committed to a three-month consultation period for a dedicated Data Centre National Policy Statement (NPS). This statement is designed to establish the national need for major developments and provide clarity on planning decisions.The original consultation deadline passed in February. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said in October that the draft would be published 'in due course', followed by a public consultation.The government is also considering whether data centres should receive Critical National Priority (CNP) status, an option raised in a November policy paper. CNP status, already applied to low-carbon energy infrastructure, gives greater weight to the need for qualifying developments during planning assessments.Applying a similar approach to data centres could strengthen the case for approving major projects, although it would not guarantee planning permission. Environmental safeguards would also remain.Parliament backed the extension of the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIP) regime to data centres in November 2025, with changes effective from January 2026. Developers can now request that nationally significant data centre projects enter the NSIP regime, allowing national rather than local planning determination.However, the dedicated policy statement intended to guide these NSIP decisions remains unpublished. This leaves the government’s position on giving major data centres additional planning weight unresolved.

stories.title: Siemens and Nvidia advance industrial AI for data center optimisation
stories.summary: Siemens and Nvidia are expanding their partnership to apply industrial AI in product design and the construction of AI factories. This collaboration leverages physics-based digital twin technology to optimise energy use and inform grid assessments for data centers.
stories.content:
Siemens and Nvidia are advancing industrial AI applications for product design, production, and the development of AI factories, according to a joint statement. The companies are delivering new products and reporting results from joint projects, ten months after expanding their partnership at CES.The collaboration focuses on designing chips that enable AI, with Siemens and Nvidia developing AI agents to automate complex chip design tasks. These agents verify results using Siemens' electronic design automation (EDA) tools and Nvidia AI infrastructure.This work extends to electrical and thermal analysis. Siemens' AI-driven electrothermal workflow predicts heat buildup and its impact on chip performance before manufacturing.Nvidia CUDA-X libraries accelerate thermal simulation, helping engineers evaluate design alternatives faster. This workflow can set up multiple tools in under five minutes, enabling 50 times more design exploration than manual methods.
### AI Factory Infrastructure

Siemens provides electrical distribution, protection, automation, and controls for the Nvidia DSX architecture, from grid connection to the AI rack. This includes the digital twin used to design, build, and operate facilities as one system.Siemens, Nvidia, and ecosystem partners have introduced the Nvidia DSX Vera Rubin Reference Design for the U.S. and European markets. These architectures translate Nvidia DSX requirements into deployable power and controls infrastructure, adapting to local standards.Siemens and Delta co-designed prefabricated, factory-tested electrical power modules. These modules can reduce data center time to market by up to 50 per cent.Siemens' physics-based digital twin, developed with Nvidia using Nvidia Omniverse libraries, helps operators plan and optimise infrastructure. Before construction, the digital twin shows grid interaction, potential cooling shortfalls, and noise impact from equipment.Operators can identify bottlenecks, evaluate infrastructure tradeoffs, and test noise-reduction measures before capital commitment. The digital twin also provides utilities with visibility for grid-connection assessments. During operation, connected telemetry and simulation help improve cooling and electricity use.

stories.title: Nxera, Sembcorp ink deal for green energy supply to Nxera data centers
stories.summary: Nxera Singapore (Nxera), the AI data center arm of Singtel Group and Sembcorp Utilities Pte Ltd, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Sembcorp Industries (Sembcorp), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for the supply of renewable and low-carbon energy to Nxera’s data centers in Singapore. The collaboration brings together Nxera’s data center expertise and Sembcorp’s energy capabilities to […]
stories.content:
Nxera Singapore (Nxera), the AI data center arm of Singtel Group and Sembcorp Utilities Pte Ltd, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Sembcorp Industries (Sembcorp), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for the supply of renewable and low-carbon energy to Nxera’s data centers in Singapore.

The collaboration brings together Nxera’s data center expertise and Sembcorp’s energy capabilities to explore solutions to support Singapore’s digitisation while reducing its carbon footprint, according to Sembcorp’s press release yesterday.

Potential solutions include low-carbon hydrogen-based generation, biomethane-based power generation, vertical building-applied photovoltaics and renewable energy imports from the 2.2GWp floating solar project at Linggiu Reservoir in Johor, Malaysia.

The MOU was signed in the presence of Dr Tan See Leng, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), Singapore and Datuk Amar Haji Fadillah bin Haji Yusof, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Transition and Water Transformation, Malaysia.

Koh Chiap Khiong, President & CEO, Gas and Related Services and CEO of Singapore, Sembcorp, said, “As AI adoption accelerates globally, demand for reliable, scalable and lower-carbon energy continues to grow. With a proven track record of powering the data centre sector, Sembcorp is well-positioned to support this growth through our diversified energy portfolio. Our partnership with Nxera further affirms our shared ambition to enable the next generation of digital infrastructure while advancing the global energy transition.”

Bill Chang, CEO of Nxera and Singtel’s Digital InfraCo unit said, “AI is driving a step-change in the power needs of data centres, and in a land- and resource-constrained market like Singapore, how we source that power matters. Working with Sembcorp gives us more options to power our growth sustainably and responsibly. Strengthening our energy resilience will be critical to underpinning Nxera’s long-term development in Singapore while supporting Singapore’s digital ambitions.”

stories.title: Iran war boosts Malaysian data centre appeal, SD Guthrie says
stories.summary: The South-east Asian nation is expected to attract more interest as a hub for the facilities

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic
The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
The South-east Asian nation is expected to attract more interest as a hub for the facilities

\[KUALA LUMPUR\] Malaysia is expected to attract more interest as a data centre hub following the outbreak of the US-Iran war, according to SD Guthrie, giving the palm oil giant and the country’s biggest landowner an opportunity to capitalise on the boom.

Even before the Middle East conflict, Malaysia was already drawing data centre investment from companies including Alphabet’s Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

Over the weekend, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Masayoshi Son of SoftBank Group chose locations in the country for US$50 billion in technology investments.

While the war was notcited as a factor in Son’s investment, SD Guthrie president and group chief executive officer Mohd Haris Mohd Arshad said Malaysia was the “most stable country” in South-east Asia for building data centres.

The world’s biggest palm oil planter by acreage previously flagged plans to use some of its lower-yielding land for industrial development to tap into the data centre boom.

The Middle East had been particularly attractive for data centre investment because of its abundant energy options, but the war has heightened risks in the region, Haris said during an interview on Friday (Oct 23), his first with foreign media since taking the helm in January.

“If you’re gonna build data centres for US$10 billion, you’re not gonna put it in a place where you might be bombed,” he said. “We are riding that wave of investment that is coming into” Malaysia, Haris added.

A large share of data centre investment flowing into Malaysia has been earmarked for Johor, which is adjacent to land-constrained Singapore.

But as investment pledges roll in, Haris warned that energy constraints will need to be addressed for the region to realise its full potential.

Data centres have signed agreements with Malaysia’s power utility Tenaga Nasional for as much as 8.77 gigawatts of peak demand, according to officials, equivalent to almost a third of 2025 installed capacity.

More power generation will be needed if the industry is to expand. In Johor, the centres could consume as much as 23 per cent of Peninsular Malaysia’s energy supply by 2031, according to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

SD Guthrie has over 210,000 hectares of freehold land, making the company Malaysia’s largest landowner, and has earmarked roughly 10 per cent of its current landbank for industrial development, along with renewable energy assets.

The palm oil producer expects income from industrial development to account for a third of its revenue by the end of the decade, Haris said.

## Palm oil outlook uncertain

Even as it seeks to capitalise on the data centre boom, SD Guthrie’s core palm oil business faces a more uncertain supply outlook.

Haris said Malaysian production is expected to remain steady at around 20 million tonnes in 2027 despite a severe El Niño, although dry weather across Indonesia will likely disrupt crop development and delay fruit ripening. The company operates plantations in both countries.

“The concern is in Indonesia,” said Haris, adding that haze stemming from wildfires is slowing harvesting at estates in Kalimantan and Sumatra and could weigh on productivity.

“Indonesia may potentially struggle with crop size (in 2027) and this could then become a supply problem for the industry.”

Malaysia, the world’s second-biggest grower, is currently grappling with a supply glut but Haris sees stockpiles starting to decline by February or March, helping to support prices.

He expects benchmark palm oil futures to climb to around RM5,000 (US$1,224) a tonne by the end of the first quarter of 2027 on slowing output and firm demand. They are currently near RM4,800 a tonne.

SD Guthrie is keen to expand in Indonesia even as greater state control over the commodities sector creates some “uncertainty and angst” among producers, Haris said.

The company’s operations have not been disrupted by the policy shifts, he added, which include plans for centralised export controls.

“I would be willing to double down on Indonesia, with the right assets to acquire and with the right partners,” Haris said. “It may not be in upstream, but I’m quite interested to look at downstream.” BLOOMBERG

stories.title: AirTrunk secures AU$4.25bn green loan for Sydney data centre campus
stories.summary: AirTrunk has secured AU$4.25 billion (US$2.8bn) in green financing to fund the continued development of its SYD3 data centre campus in Western Sydney. The announcement comes at a time when the industry is facing a more uncertain environment for data centre equity markets. The loan will support the ongoing development of SYD3, which is under […]
stories.content:
AirTrunk has secured AU$4.25 billion (US$2.8bn) in green financing to fund the continued development of its SYD3 data centre campus in Western Sydney. The announcement comes at a time when the industry is facing a more uncertain environment for data centre equity markets.

The loan will support the ongoing development of SYD3, which is under construction and expected to be completed by mid-2028. AirTrunk said the project would provide infrastructure for cloud, artificial intelligence and enterprise services, and support more than 10,000 jobs across construction, trades, engineering, logistics and safety.

The financing was backed by a consortium of 32 local and international financial institutions, with 14 banks underwriting the facility. It brings AirTrunk’s total committed debt financing to approximately AU$38.4 billion globally, including more than AU$19.8 billion across its Australian projects.

The green loan includes margin adjustments, with any contributions from financing-related savings directed to AirTrunk’s social impact programme. The company said construction measures at SYD3 include lower-carbon steel and concrete, alongside a target to divert at least 90 percent of non-hazardous construction waste from landfill.

“SYD3 is a long-term investment in Western Sydney and Australia’s digital capability, backed by the confidence of leading Australian and international banks,” said Tom Mackellar, AirTrunk’s vice president of origination and market expansion.

The company said its Australian platform comprises five campuses with more than 1.2GW of capacity. It has invested more than AU$12 billion in Australian projects to date and plans to invest a further AU$75 billion over the next decade.

### Market jitters

The financing comes as AirTrunk continues to access debt markets to fund growth across Asia Pacific, while its plans to raise capital through an equity listing have encountered a less favourable market. In October, the company postponed a planned Singapore real estate investment trust (REIT) initial public offering that could raise around US$1.5 billion, according to media reports.

The listing had been targeted for September or October but was put on hold amid market volatility and a sell-off in technology and AI stocks. AirTrunk has not announced a new launch date, although reports said it was aiming for a listing in early 2027.

AirTrunk has also secured substantial financing for its Japanese operations. In March, it announced a ¥191.6 billion (US$1.24bn) green loan to refinance existing debt and fund further development of its TOK1 campus in eastern Tokyo. The company said the campus could ultimately scale beyond 300MW, with construction underway on a phase adding more than 100MW of IT capacity.

At SYD3, AirTrunk said the green financing will support its target of net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2030 through measures including energy efficiency, renewable energy matching and lower-carbon technologies. The company is also targeting reductions in Scope 3 emissions associated with construction materials.

The expansion is being led by Australian construction firm A W Edwards. AirTrunk said it would continue working with local contractors, suppliers and community partners as the project progresses.

stories.title: AirTrunk Secures A$4.25B Green Loan For SYD3 Western Sydney Expansion: Supporting Australia’s Digital Economy
stories.summary: Asia Pacific and Middle East (APME) hyperscale data centre specialist, AirTrunk, has secured a A$4.25 billion green loan to fund the continued development of its SYD3 campus in Western Sydney. The project will add secure, resilient infrastructure for cloud, artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital services used by Australian businesses, governments and communities. The project […] The post AirTrunk Secures A$4.25B Green Loan For SYD3 Western Sydney Expansion: Supporting Australia’s…
stories.content:
Asia Pacific and Middle East (APME) hyperscale data centre specialist, AirTrunk, has secured a A$4.25 billion green loan to fund the continued development of its SYD3 campus in Western Sydney.

The project will add secure, resilient infrastructure for cloud, artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital services used by Australian businesses, governments and communities. The project is expected to support more than 10,000 jobs across construction, trades, engineering, logistics and safety.

The facility is structured as a green loan with margin adjustments. Any contributions from the margin savings on the facility will be directed to AirTrunk’s social impact program to support local charities working across STEM education, digital equity, biodiversity and conservation, sustainable innovation and disaster relief.

### Growing Western Sydney’s workforce and supply chain

SYD3 is creating project activity and opportunities for contractors and suppliers across Western Sydney and Australia, including in steel and precast manufacturing, freight and logistics, civil works, and electrical and mechanical services.

AirTrunk’s broader supplier network reflects the scale of its activity across the region. In FY26, AirTrunk worked with 1,436 supplier entities across APAC, including 615 in Australia, which accounted for A$3.4 billion in supplier activity.

For SYD3, AirTrunk is leveraging a 25,000 sqm strategic buffer zone in Western Sydney to store, stage and pre-commission critical data centre equipment, supporting just-in-time deliveries to campus. Moreover, AirTrunk’s investment in dedicated time-charter vessels further strengthens the supply chain into Port Botany, Port Kembla and beyond, creating a laser focused flow of equipment from country of origin to destination.

**Tom Mackellar, Vice President, Origination & Market Expansion said:** “SYD3 is a long-term investment in Western Sydney and Australia’s digital capability, backed by the confidence of leading Australian and international banks. As the campus develops, it’s building a regional ecosystem through active hiring, sustained project activity and strategic supply chain partnerships – creating opportunities for local workers, contractors and businesses while delivering infrastructure Australians increasingly rely on. The green financing also reflects our view that sustainability should be built into how digital infrastructure is funded and delivered. We’re focused on responsible growth that creates lasting value for communities in the regions where we operate.”

As SYD3 progresses, AirTrunk will continue to work with local contractors, suppliers and community partners while supporting the development of Australia’s digital infrastructure workforce through apprenticeships and technical skills development. AirTrunk is helping advance practical, outcomes-focused approaches to long-term workforce capability, including flexible apprenticeship pathways, partnerships with vocational education providers and post-trade upskilling through its participation in a national skills advisory group.

### Building Australia’s digital capacity responsibly

SYD3 will add capacity for cloud, AI and enterprise services – the secure computing and storage infrastructure behind digital systems used every day across business, government, education and essential services.

AirTrunk’s Australian platform spans five campuses, with more than 1.2GW of capacity. The company has invested over A$12 billion across its Australian projects to date and plans to invest a further A$75 billion over the next decade.

This deal brings AirTrunk’s total committed debt financing to \~A$38.4 billion (\~US$26.9 billion) globally, including more than A$19.8 billion across its Australian projects.

The financing supports AirTrunk’s Net Zero 2030 target of net zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2030 through measures including energy efficiency, renewable energy matching and lower-carbon technologies, while driving progressive reductions in Scope 3 emissions through lower embodied carbon across new data centre builds. At SYD3, construction measures include the use of lower carbon steel and concrete, as well as a target to divert at least 90 per cent of non-hazardous construction waste from landfill.

Construction of the expanded SYD3 development, led by A W Edwards, is underway, with completion expected by mid-2028.

### Strong lender backing for SYD3 expansion

A consortium of 32 local and international financial institutions backed the green loan, making it one of the largest lending groups assembled for a data centre financing in Australia.

The green loan was underwritten by 14 lead banks: Banco Santander, S.A.; BNP Paribas; Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank; DBS Bank Ltd.; Deutsche Bank; ING Bank N.V.; Mizuho Bank, Ltd.; MUFG Bank, Ltd.; National Australia Bank Limited; Royal Bank of Canada, Société Générale; Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation; The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited; and United Overseas Bank Limited.

Green Loan Coordinators were: Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation; The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited; and United Overseas Bank Limited.

Legal advisers for the transaction were Mallesons (Borrowers Counsel) and Gilbert & Tobin (Lenders Counsel).

stories.title: Ecoblox partners with Rimac on modular data center solution
stories.summary: First deployment slated for Rimac's campus in Kerestinec, Croatia
stories.content:
Modular data center builder Ecoblox has partnered with Croatian electric vehicle manufacturer Rimac to develop and deliver a modular data center solution.

The companies signed a Joint Development Agreement to integrate Rimac Technology’s battery and power electronics with Ecoblox’s AI infrastructure, MDC architecture, design, and hardware/software system integration to deliver a high-density modular data center solution.

The modular data center will integrate Rimac’s UNI battery modules, which the companies claim will enable longer continuous backup power for critical computing hardware. The integration will include Rimac’s battery management system, which will provide Ecoblox with real-time monitoring and control to manage the modular unit.

Rimac’s UNI battery modules are designed for use across automotive, energy storage, marine, off-highway, commercial, and industrial applications. This deployment will be the first time they are used in data center infrastructure.

The first modular data center is expected to be completed in November and will be sited at the Rimac campus in Kerestinec, Croatia.

"Partnering with Rimac Technology allows us to redefine high-density power delivery for the next generation of AI compute," said Doug Makishima, CEO at Ecoblox. "By integrating automotive-grade energy storage and power electronics directly into our modular data center architecture, we are removing grid constraints and enabling cloud providers and enterprise customers to deploy scalable, power-resilient AI clusters faster and more efficiently than ever before."

Nurdin Pitarevic, CEO of Rimac Technology, added: "Our battery and power electronics technologies have been developed and industrialized to meet some of the most demanding requirements in the automotive industry. The same capabilities are increasingly relevant to high-power AI infrastructure, where power density, thermal management, safety, and reliability are critical. Together with Ecoblox, we are applying these technologies to a new high-power application and bringing automotive-grade technology to AI data centers."

Ecoblox is headquartered in Dubai, UAE, and offers a range of solutions, from rack-level to 20-40 ft modular data centers, plus custom module data centers, all designed for high-density workloads and compatible with Nvidia and AMD GPUs. The company claims that it can deploy the data centers in less than eight months.

stories.title: Cadence unveils Nvidia-powered AI data center in Munich, Germany
stories.summary: Facility will support electronic design automation (EDA), simulation, and offer sovereign AI cloud services
stories.content:
Cadence has launched a sovereign AI data center in Munich, Germany, that supports the company’s OnCloud and Reality Digital Twin platforms, alongside the Cadence Millennium M2000 AI Supercomputer.

Powered by Nvidia Vera and Grace CPUs and Blackwell GPUs, Cadence said the data center provides “secure, European sovereign cloud infrastructure” for electronic design automation (EDA), simulation, and AI workloads.

The facility is certified to ISO 27001, ISO 27017, and SOC 2 Type II standards, and will expand Cadence's European cloud footprint. The data center will complement existing European cloud resources, including leading public cloud provider infrastructure in Frankfurt.

The company’s Reality Digital Twin platform allows customers to design, validate, and optimize next-generation AI infrastructure before deployment, with Cadence stating it will use the platform within the Munich facility to improve the design and operation of its compute infrastructure, boost energy efficiency, and reduce operational risk.

“Europe's semiconductor and system design community requires secure infrastructure that enables innovation without compromising data sovereignty,” said Paul Scannell, SVP of the global customer success team at Cadence. “By combining Nvidia Vera and Grace CPU platforms with the Cadence Millennium M2000 Supercomputer and making these capabilities available through Cadence OnCloud, we are providing European engineering teams with the compute, design intelligence and flexibility needed to build the next generation of AI-driven chips and systems.”

“Chip designs and AI infrastructure are strategic assets for European industry, and sovereignty means being able to develop both while protecting the data behind them,” said Tim Costa, VP and GM of industrial and computational engineering at Nvidia. “With Cadence, we’re bringing NVIDIA accelerated computing into European cloud-based design workflows and Omniverse libraries into AI factory simulation. Companies can design the silicon and validate the infrastructure to run it – from power delivery to cooling – within a European environment built to protect their design data.”

Cadence OnCloud on sovereign infrastructure is available today to European customers, with additional compute capabilities, including Nvidia Vera and Grace and CPU systems, the Cadence Millennium M2000 AI Supercomputer, and Cadence Reality Digital Twin Platform instances, planned as part of the ongoing expansion of the Munich data center.

stories.title: Sponsored: The next evolution of data center backup power
stories.summary: Building flexibility from the engine up
stories.content:
As AI and HPC workloads drive rising demand for power capacity, resilience, and uptime, data center operators are focused on how to power, cool, and scale high-density racks as infrastructure requirements evolve. Yet while flexibility within the white space is a critical consideration, is equal attention being given to the adaptability of the backup power infrastructure supporting it?

Backup power architecture can easily be regarded as secondary to the more visible infrastructure within the data hall. After all, these systems are designed to remain on standby, ready to take over when the primary power supply fails. But as AI makes predicting future capacity requirements more challenging, backup power infrastructure's flexibility and scalability deserve as much attention as the systems it protects.

## AI is changing the backup power equation

The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports that global data center electricity consumption is projected to almost double, from 485TWh in 2025 to approximately 950TWh by 2030, with electricity consumption from AI-focused facilities expected to triple over the same period.

As power demand grows, so too does pressure on electricity networks. Grid connection constraints, combined with uncertainty over future power availability, create additional challenges for operators. It is therefore important to consider not just how much backup power a facility needs today, but how to expand that capacity as requirements change.

Enterprise data centers must accommodate increasingly power-intensive workloads within existing facilities. At the same time, hyperscale operators must plan for rapidly growing capacity in existing and new-build facilities, often adding capacity in phases. Meanwhile, neocloud providers delivering GPU-intensive AI computing capacity face additional pressure to deploy and scale infrastructure rapidly.

Across all these environments, the challenge is not just providing sufficient backup generation, but determining exactly how much capacity to deploy, when to deploy it, and how to accommodate future growth without unnecessary overprovisioning.

## Rethinking backup power architecture

Traditionally, many data centers have relied on having centralized backup power configurations, using fewer, larger generator sets to provide the capacity needed during an outage. Where power requirements are relatively predictable and significant expansion isn't anticipated, this approach may be entirely appropriate.

However, for expanding enterprise facilities, phased hyperscale developments, and AI-focused data centers, where future capacity requirements may be less predictable, distributed architectures incorporating multiple smaller generator sets offer a more flexible alternative. With these units operating in parallel, operators can add backup power capacity in stages as demand grows, rather than committing to larger increments upfront.

This principle is already familiar across other areas of data center infrastructure. Modular UPS systems, cooling equipment, and power distribution solutions increasingly allow operators to add capacity as demand grows. Applying the same thinking to backup generation gives operators more choice over how and when they deploy additional power infrastructure.

While the best approach depends on the facility's capacity requirements, expansion plans, and overall infrastructure design, the engines powering the generator sets play a critical role in supporting the performance and adaptability of the backup power system. Their reliability, power output, load acceptance, efficiency, and serviceability all affect how effectively backup generation can be delivered, maintained, and scaled.

## Five benefits of distributed backup power architectures

### 1. Greater flexibility for phased capacity expansion

Rather than committing to large increments of backup generation capacity upfront, distributed architectures allow operators to add smaller generator sets as demand grows. By using engines that deliver the required power output in a compact footprint, genset manufacturers can develop modular solutions that let operators expand capacity in stages, avoid unnecessary overprovisioning and align investment more closely with actual requirements.

Smaller engines can also be easier to transport and deliver to site. Their compact size often means they can be transported on standard trucks rather than requiring specialist transport. This can help avoid road closures or overnight deliveries, reducing transport costs and delivery times.

### 2. Improved resilience through multiple generator sets

Distributing backup generation across multiple generator sets increases resilience by reducing dependence on individual large units, so the failure of one generator set need not compromise the facility's required backup power capacity, provided the system includes sufficient redundancy. However, the engines also play an important role: reliable starting, rapid load acceptance, and fast response to changing power demands are essential to maintaining backup power when needed.

### 3. More precise capacity matching and load management

A multi-engine architecture allows generating capacity to match operational requirements more closely. Rather than relying on a single large generator operating at a relatively low load, operators can potentially run an appropriate number of smaller units. Efficient engine performance, supported by electronic engine management systems, can help optimize fuel consumption and maintain reliable operation, particularly during extended periods of backup power operation.

### 4. Greater maintenance flexibility and operational continuity

Distributed backup power systems can offer greater maintenance flexibility, allowing individual generator sets to be serviced while others remain available, provided sufficient backup capacity is maintained. Engines designed for robustness and ease of servicing, with accessible components and advanced diagnostics, can further simplify maintenance, help extend engine service life, and support long-term operational reliability.

### 5. Future readiness and integration with emerging technologies

As data center energy strategies evolve, distributed architectures can offer opportunities to incorporate new technologies alongside existing generation infrastructure. Engines compatible with renewable fuels such as HVO, together with natural gas alternatives, can provide greater choice for meeting changing energy requirements.

Advanced engine management systems can also work alongside battery energy storage and intelligent power management systems to support hybrid power solutions, offering greater flexibility in how energy is generated, stored and managed.

## Engine technology at the heart of future backup power

The next evolution of data center backup power will not be defined by generating capacity alone, but by how effectively that capacity can be deployed, maintained and adapted as requirements change.

Engine manufacturers play a key role in this transition. Volvo Penta, for example, offers a range of high-performance backup power generator engines that enable genset manufacturers to develop reliable backup power solutions for different capacity requirements and configurations. Backed by Volvo Group’s automotive-scale manufacturing capabilities, its engines are developed for dependable load acceptance, fuel efficiency, and long-term durability, with compact designs and simplified maintenance that help support the development of more flexible, efficient, and resilient backup power infrastructure.

As AI continues to reshape data center requirements, the question is no longer how much backup generation capacity operators need, but how to configure that capacity to deliver resilience today while accommodating future growth.

stories.title: Anthropic files S-1 for IPO, with $417bn in compute commitments
stories.summary: Data center costs spread over the next 20 years
stories.content:
Anthropic is set to go public and has filed its S-1 IPO paperwork.

The generative AI firm revealed several details about its operations in its 335-page filing, including some stats about its growing data center footprint.

Anthropic reported that revenue grew 1,300 percent in the first half of the year, to total $16.3 billion. In the same timeframe, it reported a net loss of $80.7bn - however, it said that $72.4bn of that loss was due to a one-off accounting charge.

In the first half of the year, the company's operating losses shrank to $693 million from $2.1bn for the same period of 2025. It reported $6.2bn in debt.

The majority of its costs came in mounting compute commitments, with the company noting that "expected future fixed or minimum guaranteed commitments under these agreements were approximately $265.6bn with terms ranging from one to 20 years."

Anthropic said that it has "also entered into compute and infrastructure agreements that do not specify a fixed or minimum dollar commitment. Payments under these agreements will depend on the capacity made available and deployed, delivery timing, and pricing, and are not yet determinable."

While it did not detail those costs, it said that "such payments are expected to be significant."

It separately said that it had "entered into new, and amended existing, lease and commercial agreements primarily to secure additional compute and infrastructure capacity, with aggregate future minimum payment obligations of approximately $417bn," as of December 2025.

The company added: "These primarily consist of leases for compute equipment and data centers and purchase commitments with certain cloud providers, commencing between 2026 and 2027 with terms ranging from less than one year to 20 years.

"The Company also expanded certain existing commercial agreements under which it expects to secure additional compute and infrastructure capacity to be delivered between 2028 and 2031. As certain commercial terms have not yet been finalized, the Company estimates aggregate future payments under these agreements to be approximately $125bn to $150bn."

Particular compute deals mentioned include a 20-year lease for a data center yet to be constructed, an agreement to rent compute paid for with up to $42bn in convertible promissory notes, and a $500m power purchase contract in favor of the power counterparty as part of a contract with a data center provider.

In April 2026, the Company deposited $2.5bn into an escrow account in connection with a compute and infrastructure lease agreement.

Anthropic is a known customer of Google, AWS, Microsoft, SpaceXAI, Fluidstack, Nscale, Akamai, Lambda, and others.

Despite compute costs increasing, the company said that revenue per dollar of compute was improving. "For example, our revenue grew 1,368 percent year over year for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to our compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 300 percent during the same period."

Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

stories.title: Fireworks to lease data center capacity in Dallas, Texas
stories.summary: Company to lease capacity from Forum Markets/Edge Node venture
stories.content:
Forum Markets is to supply Nvidia-backed inference provider Fireworks with data center capacity in Texas.

The Nasdaq-listed company this week announced that Forum Edge AI LLC, the company's joint venture (JV) with Edge Node Inc., has entered into a definitive agreement with Fireworks for a 36-month reservation of Nvidia B300 GPU capacity at its existing, powered data center facility in Dallas.

The deal, Forum Edge's first contracted customer commitment, is valued at $94.4 million. The GPUs are expected to be deployed at Forum Edge's Dallas data center in late December or early January.

"This agreement is an important proof point for our AI infrastructure strategy and reflects our focus on bringing revenue-generating GPUs to market quickly in a modular manner," said McAndrew Rudisill, Forum Markets chairman and CEO. "We have a strong partnership with Fireworks and are excited about our growth trajectory as we scale our AI infrastructure business. This is the first finalized contract Forum Edge is executing against and the first of several exciting partnerships we expect to deploy into our unique footprint."

Founded in 2022, Fireworks provides inference, training, and routing that help enterprises deploy and scale generative AI applications in production. The company was most recently valued at approximately $17.5 billion, with backers including Nvidia, Atreides Management, Index Ventures, and TCV.

The company rents GPU servers from other sources, and then sells access to open-source AI models, competing with the likes of Together AI and Baseten. Last year, Oracle revealed that it counts Fireworks AI among its customers. The company also uses GPUs from Voltage Park. On its website, Fireworks says it operates across 30 global regions across Europe, North America, and Asia Pacific.

Investment firm Forum Markets announced a partnership with Edge Node Inc. earlier this month. The JV initial portfolio consists of 2MW of a 4MW data center in Dallas; a 9MW data center campus in High Point, North Carolina; and one initial mobile communications tower site of 1-2MW.

Full details haven't been shared, but the Dallas data center currently offers 2MW, operated by Edge Node AI, with another 2MW coming later this year or early next year and allocated to the joint venture.

Forum Markets is an asset manager that was previously focused on “tokenization of institutional-grade real-world assets on Ethereum.” Today the firm describes itself as investing in cash-generating assets across AI infrastructure, commercial aerospace, manufactured housing finance, and auto credit.

Founded last year, Texas-based Edge Node is a ‘Tokens-as-a-Service’ provider, aiming to offer low-latency compute and inference services and access to LLMs in the US. The company has yet to launch its services.

stories.title: Karman completes power orchestration pilot at NextGen data center in Montreal, Canada
stories.summary: To extend software rollout across NextGen's European operations
stories.content:
Karman has deployed its AI-enabled power orchestration software at a NextGen Cloud data center in Montreal, Canada.

According to the company, the software enabled 16 Nvidia B300 servers to operate within the power budget provisioned for ten servers. This, the company said, delivered 60 percent more nameplate compute capacity and token throughput while maintaining inference quality and reliability. Karman claimed that the technology maintained this performance under a range of workloads, including those with sustained high-power workloads.

The initial partnership was announced back in March, with its stated aim to increase the available AI compute capacity within NexGen's already deployed data center footprint, maximizing its capacity in a grid-constrained environment. According to the partners, following the successful demonstration, the companies have now extended the software rollout across NexGen’s European cloud operations.

“As demand for AI compute continues to accelerate, efficiency is becoming just as important as capacity. The results we’ve achieved with Karman demonstrate that we can deliver significantly more compute from our existing infrastructure without requiring additional provisioned power,” said Chris Starkey, CEO of NexGen Cloud.

“This creates a compelling opportunity to improve infrastructure utilization, accelerate deployment, and ultimately deliver greater value to our customers. We’re excited to build on these results as we expand our partnership across Europe.”

Karman’s platform utilizes AI to provide real-time visibility for grid operators and data center firms. It works by identifying and managing distributed energy resources, which it claims enhances resiliency and offsets the need for future infrastructure investments. The platform can integrate with smart meters, providing AI solutions for utility companies and their customers.

The company developed the platform using a custom version of the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, an Edge AI platform, which it claims provides 100 times the processing power of other meter-based solutions. The platform can connect to millions of endpoints and coordinate them to monitor and react to real-time conditions.

“The fastest, low-cost way to scale AI today is by getting more compute out of the infrastructure already built,” said Josh Brumberger, Karman CEO.

“Data centers hold power in reserve for worst-case scenarios that rarely happen. Karman turns that stranded capacity into usable compute. We’re excited to bring this value to NexGen Cloud and their customers.”

Karman was rebranded earlier this month, formerly operating under the name Utilidata. Also this month, the company partnered with French industrial group Legrand to integrate Karman into its data center power distribution product lines.

In June, the firm raised $60.3 million in Series C funding to scale its platform, led by Renown Capital Partners, with participation from Quanta, Nvidia, and existing investor Keyframe Capital.

stories.title: Theft of AI equipment hits $150m in 2026, with fraud responsible for 92% of incidents – report
stories.summary: Reports of stolen data center equipment up 34 percent since 2024, cargo risk management firm Overhaul said
stories.content:
More than $150 million worth of AI equipment has been stolen this year, a report from cargo risk management firm Overhaul has detailed.

According to the company, individual losses regularly exceed $30m, and such thefts occur weekly.

However, it should be noted that details regarding the underlying incident count, geographic coverage, or shipment volume against which that increase was measured were not disclosed in the report.

Reports of stolen data center equipment, compute components, and semiconductors are up 34 percent since 2024, Overhaul said, with the primary method of theft shifting from force to fraud – deception, such as the use of false carrier identities, altered paperwork, or spoofed communications, featured in 92 percent of the high value technology shipment thefts Overhaul analyzed.

One incident included in the report involved $60m-worth of hardware belonging to an unnamed company being redirected to an unauthorized location, although in this instance the firm was alerted to the attempted theft and able to recover its goods.

Earlier this year, the Washington Post detailed a separate incident from July 2025 when an individual stole $9.5m-worth of Apple products, and AMD chips worth $6m.

While Overhaul noted that impacted companies will likely be insured against stolen equipment and hardware, insurance will not cover indirect losses related to timeline disruptions or delayed customer contracts.

This week, The Information reported that data center late fees were now hitting around $5m a day, up from approximately $1m in spring of this year. Meanwhile, insurance company Swiss Re has forecast that data center insurance premiums could approach $24 billion by 2030, with S&P Global estimating that figure currently sits around $10bn, double that of the global aviation insurance market.

stories.title: Generative Bionics plans AI data center and humanoid robotics factory in Italy
stories.summary: Could form first part of physical AI factory network
stories.content:
Robotics firm Generative Bionics is planning to build an AI data center in Italy as part of a facility to help develop its humanoid robots for industrial settings.

The 5,000 sqm (53,820 sq ft) facility, dubbed the Physical AI Data Factory, is designed to “move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment and to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models and know-how behind Europe's industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent,” the company said.

Generative Bionics plans to build the data center at an undisclosed location in the Liguria region of Italy, where it is based. Though IT capacity for the site has not been disclosed, the company said it will run on AMD Helios infrastructure, and that the site could be partially operational by Q4 2027.

It will allow fleets of the company’s first robot Gene.01, to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. “These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behaviour and task execution, before deployment at customer sites,” Generative Bionics said.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin, so tasks can be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle, the company explained.

"We are replicating the world, physically and digitally, to train humanoid robots at scale before they ever enter it," said Daniele Pucci, CEO of Generative Bionics. "The physical AI data factory is how we do it: fleets of Gene.01 learn from real industrial work, we stress-test those skills across thousands of digital-twin variations on AMD compute, and we return validated world action models to the field.

“This is the infrastructure that enables the action intelligence layer of physical AI in real customer environments. With AMD at our side since day one, on board Gene.01 and now at the heart of the data factory, we are building this network here in Europe, so that the data, the models and the infrastructure behind our industrial humanoids are developed and operated on the continent."

Generative Bionics was founded to commercialize physical AI research from the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia. To date, it has raised €70 million ($78m) from backers including AMD.

It hopes to build a second factory elsewhere in Europe, and a third outside the continent to serve global markets.

AMD will provide high-performance AI computing infrastructure to support the development of the factory, deploying its double-width Helios rack-scale system, which has been designed specifically for AI hardware. The infrastructure is expected to deliver the scalable compute capabilities needed for AI model training, processing physical and synthetic data, and running digital-twin simulations.

"Physical AI represents an exciting opportunity to bring the power of AI into the real world, creating new possibilities for automation and industrial innovation," said Keith Strier, SVP, global AI markets at AMD. "With AMD Helios powering Italy's first physical AI data factory, we are providing scalable, high-performance computing infrastructure needed to turn that potential into reality. Our collaboration with Generative Bionics marks an important step in advancing European AI and industrial sovereignty, enabling the development and deployment of next-generation intelligent robotics applications while strengthening Europe's capacity to innovate."

stories.title: Nvidia backs open standards for AI factory builds
stories.summary: The move could let data centre builders use common blueprints for high-power AI systems, easing deployment of racks up to 250kW.
stories.content:
Tue, 27th Oct 2026 (Today)
NVIDIA has contributed Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to the Open Compute Project through its MGX architecture, as part of a broader push to establish open standards for AI infrastructure.

It also unveiled new open source software for its DSX AI Factory platform and announced separate networking and power infrastructure efforts with partners including Meta, Cisco, Google and Visionbay.

### Open designs

NVIDIA said its latest MGX 1.2 specification extends its open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar for higher-power AI systems. It also adds support for native 19-inch equipment and denser rack designs.

The updated design is intended to give system builders a common framework for AI data centre infrastructure based on the Vera Rubin generation of products. NVIDIA said the architecture supports rack deployments of up to 250kW.

NVIDIA also outlined a Vera CPU rack design based on the same third-generation MGX rack architecture. It said the system is aimed at workloads including tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution for AI agents, alongside larger-scale training and inference systems built on Vera Rubin NVL72.

### Software layer

Alongside the hardware contribution, NVIDIA released open source software components for DSX OS, the operating layer within its DSX AI Factory platform. The additions cover network configuration, cluster validation, rack management and bare-metal provisioning.

The tools include NVIDIA Config Manager, Cluster Readiness Engine, Rack Management Service and a Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller. NVIDIA said the software draws on its experience operating DGX Cloud and is intended for cloud providers and software partners running multi-tenant platforms.

### Industry standards

NVIDIA also joined AMD, Google and Meta in publishing Open Data Centre Specification v0.7, which sets out a common approach to facility design for large AI installations, including power architecture, cooling infrastructure and physical layout.

A separate Grid Resilience Specification, published by Google, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, sets expectations for how large AI facilities should respond during utility grid disturbances. According to NVIDIA, it covers staying connected to the grid, responding automatically and returning to near-full load in less than two seconds.

NVIDIA argued that open specifications would allow equipment manufacturers, colocation providers and data centre operators to design and build infrastructure without relying on customer-specific proprietary designs.

### Power systems

Power distribution was another focus of the announcements. Visionbay introduced plans for K-1, an AI factory platform based on an 800 VDC architecture and designed with future Vera Rubin deployments in mind.

NVIDIA said the design combines its 800 VDC reference architecture with power and thermal systems from Vertiv. The approach centres on cluster-level power centres that convert AC to DC and distribute 800 VDC closer to compute resources, as operators contend with higher rack power densities.

The design is intended to reduce the need for additional copper, cabling and power-conversion equipment associated with lower-voltage power distribution. It would also allow operators to introduce 800 VDC in stages rather than through a full redesign.

### Networking push

In networking, Meta said it is adopting NVIDIA Spectrum-6 102.4Tb/s Ethernet switches for larger Vera Rubin AI factory deployments. NVIDIA said the switches provide double the switching capacity and per-lane bandwidth of Spectrum-4.

Meta's switch, called N-IceCube, will run the Facebook Open Switching System, or FBOSS, the company's open source network operating system. NVIDIA said FBOSS is built on the Switch Abstraction Interface, an Open Compute Project standard it helped develop.

The collaboration also centres on Spectrum-X Multiplane technology, which distributes GPU traffic across up to eight independent network planes. NVIDIA said this is intended to support AI factory deployments of more than 100,000 GPUs with fewer switch tiers.

Meta provided the only direct quote in the announcements. "We are excited about our close partnership with NVIDIA in making multiplane fabrics operationally scalable and performant, a critical requirement both for our own infrastructure builds and for our joint cloud partners," said Omar Baldonado, Senior Director of Data Centre and AI Networking at Meta. "Extending FBOSS to Spectrum ASICs means we can run that same software stack across our fabrics, and Meta's new Spectrum-based switch, N-IceCube, brings that into Icepack - our liquid-cooled 102.4T network rack for scale-out that connects upcoming generations of accelerators in our fleet."

NVIDIA and Cisco also announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable standard, or USFP, for optical transceivers. They said the format is designed to provide a path to 400Gb/s-per-lane networking while keeping a footprint similar to current OSFP modules.

According to NVIDIA, USFP packs 16 full-duplex lanes, with plans to scale to 32, offering four times the bandwidth density of conventional 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable optics. The companies are working with TE Connectivity and Amphenol on connectors, cages and modules.

Separately, NVIDIA and Google said future ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs will support Falcon Transport, Google's transport protocol for Ethernet networks. NVIDIA said the aim is to improve efficiency and interoperability for large-scale AI networking while allowing NVIDIA and Google network interface cards to communicate over a common transport.

stories.title: Cooler Master announces 2.5MW in-row CDU
stories.summary: PC gaming company expands data center cooling lineup
stories.content:
Cooler Master has launched a new Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) for liquid-cooled data center environments, moving it further into the data center cooling space.

The company, which historically has served the PC gaming community, recently announced a new 2.5MW liquid-to-liquid in-row CDU.

Delivering up to 2.5MW of cooling capacity at 990 GPM with a 4-5°C approach temperature difference, the company said the system enables operators to “support larger AI clusters, higher rack densities, and future infrastructure growth without compromising reliability.”

The dual-system architecture, load balancing, and centralized management can support up to 32 interconnected CDUs, scaling to 80MW. Each unit requires 40kW to operate.

Mass production is targeted for Q4 2026.

The CDU is part of Cooler Master’s range of cooling solutions for AI infrastructure, including cold plates, manifolds, and filling and commissioning tools.

The company offers liquid-to-liquid CDUs starting from 150 kW, with in-rack and in-row configurations.

The firm is also working on liquid-to-air systems to help operators host liquid-cooled servers within existing air-cooled environments. Cooler Master’s 300kW Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) CDU is already in production, while the 30kW in-rack liquid-to-air model is targeted for production in Q4 2026.

Founded in 1992, Taiwan-based Cooler Master is traditionally focused on cooling and power equipment for consumer personal computing.

The company announced it was expanding further into the data center space over the summer, with a focus on Nvidia’s MGX modular reference design architecture.

The company said it is also working on two-phase cooling offerings.

stories.content:
Africa has developed an appetite for digital services. From education, to health, to financial services, and financial markets, the continent’s young population is driving the need to meet demand for these services.

Despite this demand, many African nations lack the capacity for digital services, especially when data sovereignty laws dictate that information required by these services remain in-country. African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat Secretary-General Wamkele Mene said in July that by the end of 2035, 700 data centers would be needed to process and manage the data of citizens on the continent.

In a bid to meet that call MTN Group, one of Africa’s largest telecommunications providers, announced in August that its Digital Infrastructure arm, also known as Bayobab, would be establishing a joint venture called Africa Data Hub Holding. The firm partnered with a UAE-based data center investment platform founded by Tarek Al Ashram. This new venture would be tasked with building AI-enabled data centers with a total capacity of 150 MW in Africa, and the MTN believes the best place to start is South Africa and Nigeria.

Both of these markets are expected to see incredible growth in their data center markets between 2026 and 2031. Research and Markets puts South Africa’s market hitting a value of US$ 5.28 billion by 2031 while Nigeria will reach US$ 1.09 billion in the same year. Nigeria’s CAGR is pegged at 24.99 percent while South Africa’s is much lower at 12.90 percent but is the largest market on the continent today.

Mazen Mroué, MTN Digital Infrastructure Chief Executive Officer, speaking with w.media highlighted that in addition to their growth potential, Nigeria and South Africa are two of MTN’s biggest markets. In South Africa the telco has 92.2 and in Nigeria it has as many as 39.5 million customers. As the CEO tells w.media, the choice to start its data center buildout in these two nations was a condition of the MTN Group Board approving the joint venture.

“We received approval from our Group Board to proceed with this programme with three mandates: establish a partnership, start in markets we already exist in, and focus on greenfields,” says Mroué.

“MTN already owns many data centers across markets but they are mostly used by MTN for its own core services and enterprise businesses. Many of those data centers require some additional work to become AI-enabled data centers,” says Mroué.

Greenfield projects are central to Africa Data Hub’s initial strategy. While brownfield and retrofitting projects are consideration, the focus is on establishing a solid footing before taking on retrofits of brownfields.

“We are implementing the programme in two phases, beginning with a greenfield approach. Once we have established a solid foundation, demonstrated tangible progress, and achieved key strategic milestones, we will revisit the brownfield opportunity,” he continued.

#### **Pace doesn’t change the destination**

Ralph Mupita, MTN Group’s Chief Executive Officer, has said that the firm is targeting 150 MW of capacity in its first phase of the programme. South Africa’s data center capacity currently sits between 350 to 450 MW with capacity in Nigeria sitting at approximately 136 MW.

While committed to addressing the growing demand for locally accessible compute infrastructure, Mroué tells w.media that MTN is approaching its 150 MW buildout with the understanding that it will need a clear plan for how the capacity will be developed and brought to market.

“We believe there is significant market demand, and our priority is to address it through the right strategic partnerships and operating model. The 150 MW represents the first step in a longer-term plan to build data centre capacity across Africa, with the flexibility to expand as market demand evolves. Our consideration is to employ a scalable approach to building out our data centers. It depends on demand, supply, and other factors. For example if we see a surge in demand, we should be able to leverage the structure we’ve put in place to scale up and meet that demand,” says Mroué.

This will no doubt lead to a tricky balancing act for MTN and Africa Data Hub Holding which will need to meet demand while also deploying capital responsibly.

“We don’t want to rush and make big announcements. We want to build the foundation right,” Mroué added.

#### **Proof of future**

Mroué makes it clear that this project isn’t a flash in the pan for MTN. The telco was founded in Johannesburg, South Africa in 1994 at the dawn of the county’s democracy and over that time it has grown its footprint to 19 countries and it became the sixth largest telco in the world after surpassing 300 million subscribers in 2025. The company intends to apply this dedication to its data center buildout as well.

“Cloud technology is really important, but the sovereignty part is being increasingly promoted, especially in Africa. And who is the best candidate to play a role in building out sovereign infrastructure? A company that is African. An organisation that is successful in Africa. An entity with the ambition to move in the direction of AI-enabled data centers in Africa, and is able to work with partners. MTN ticks all of those boxes,” explains Mroué.

MTN’s investment in data centres goes beyond just responding to market trends. The organisation views data centres as an important part of its Ambition 2030 strategy and believes that combining its connectivity, fintech and infrastructure businesses will help meet growing demand for digital services across Africa.

“MTN’s fibre business, together with its data centre programme and the potential acquisition of tower infrastructure assets, presents a unique strategic opportunity to establish an integrated, open-access digital infrastructure platform across selected markets,“ explains Mroué.

#### **Full-stack provider**

As Mroué tells it, Africa Data Hub Holding is looking to build out infrastructure that serves the African market while also attracting international investment in multiple forms. Discussing the customers the venture hopes to attract, Mroué says hyperscalers remain a key priority, especially those looking to scale across Africa without the complexity of building and managing their own infrastructure. Equally important are enterprises and public sector institutions undergoing digital transformation, where robust digital infrastructure serves as the foundation for innovation, improved public services, greater digital inclusion, and sustainable national economic growth.

With MTN, bringing in its strong presence and robust connectivity, partnering with a platform with global experience and expertise, international players will be able to unlock growth opportunities across the continent.

Over the next 12 months Africa Data Hub Holding will start to execute on its vision. The firm will focus on moving forward with its projects in South Africa and Nigeria while also engaging with potential customers which, as mentioned, include hyperscalers and cloud providers, but will also include enterprises, and the public sector.

“Africa Data Hub Holding is a key initiative that reflects MTN’s priorities and our commitment to advancing Africa’s digital infrastructure. Through Africa Data Hub Holding, we are building a platform that can scale with demand and support the continent’s long-term digital growth,” Mroué concluded.
